catalog_quote: The distinctions between long and short vowels and distinctions between tones (whether a syllable is spoken with a higher or lower voice pitch) are both important for correct pronunciation and for distinguishing the meanings of words in Karkare. Native speakers of Karekare, however, know the correct vowel lengths and tones of words without having to see them written, and like publications in Hausa, publications in Karekare generally do not mark vowel length and tone. ... LOW TONES have a grave accent (`) over the vowel, HIGH TONES have no accent marks, FALLING TONES have a circumflex accent (^), and RISING TONES have a hachek (ˇ): HIGH: gam ‘ram’ LOW: gàm ‘many’ LOW-LOW: ɗìnkàu ‘gums’ HIGH-LOW: ɗinkàu ‘cooking’ HIGH-LOW: zinkò ‘peeping’ LOW-HIGH: zìnko ‘harvesting’ FALLING: fî ‘close!’ RISING: fǎi ‘to close’
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

new_statements.rule_in_words: Karekare is a lexical tone language: every syllable carries High or Low tone (plus falling and rising contours, falling only on heavy syllables), and tone together with vowel length distinguishes word meanings. No source on Karekare mentions word stress at all; the only stress remark is Schuh's family-level statement (A Chadic Cornucopia 2017, p. 89) that in Chadic languages prosodic prominence 'is a function of the interaction of tone, syllable weight, and intonation and plays no role that is not attributable to those properties', with Karekare listed (pp. 92-93) among the two-level-tone (H/L with downdrift) languages.
new_statements.exceptions: None about stress. Tone notes: rightward tone spreading is areal in Yobe languages (Schuh, Yobe linguistic area, fn. 13); falling tone restricted to heavy syllables (Schuh, Karekare Verb Paradigms); tone plays no role in conditioning nasal release (Schuh 2003, p. 3).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level lexical tone in dictionary citation forms; the dictionary notes final vowel-length contrasts are neutralised in isolation and surface phrase-medially. Dictionary is not dialect-specific by design.
new_statements.identity_note: Sources describe Karekare at language level (kare1348); the 2009 dictionary deliberately mixes dialects ('has not attempted to strictly adhere to forms of words from a single dialect'). Danhausa et al. 2026 describes the Kwarta Mataci (southern Pakaro/Mataci) dialect; Barde 2010 (cited there) the Jalam dialect; no dialect glottocodes exist in Glottolog 5.1. Autonym Karai-Karai; also Kerrikerri, Kerekere.

sources.note: Introduction (pp. iv-viii) gives a spelling/phonology sketch: Karekare is tonal, with High (unmarked), Low (grave), Falling (circumflex) and Rising (hacek) tones that distinguish word meanings (gam 'ram' vs gam 'many'; zinko 'peeping' vs zinko 'harvesting'); vowel length contrastive but neutralised phrase-finally. The word 'stress' never occurs; nothing on accent placement.

sources.note: Family-level, not Karekare-specific: p. 6 (original book outline) 'stress: no Chadic language has stress as a prosodic parameter'; p. 89 'All Chadic languages are tone languages.. International Journal of Religious and Interdisciplinary Studies 3(1): 1-12. doi:10.64529/w3n9qg57
sources.note: Morphology of the Kwarta Mataci dialect; sec. 4.3 documents lexical/grammatical tone contrasts (sara LH 'hand' vs saara HL 'fashionable'). No mention of stress. Cites Gamawa 2018 and Marcus 2014 (Nigerian works on Karekare morphology), Barde 2010 (Jalam dialect).

sources.citation: Schuh, Russell G. 2003 (ms; also UCLA Working Papers in Phonetics 107, 2008). Shooting Through the Nose in Karekare: A Study of Nasally Released Stops in a Chadic Language. UCLA, 18 pp.
sources.note: Phonology article; fn. 1 p. 2: grave accent = low tone, unmarked syllables bear high tone; p. 3 'the syllabic nasal bears the tone that would otherwise have been born by the vowel.. tone plays no role in the conditioning of nasal release'. 'Stress'/'unstressed' appear only about German, English and Australian languages (pp. 5, 15, 17); no statement about Karekare stress.
